Complexity should only be increased incrementally and methodically. A more complex model, like an XGBoost ensemble or a neural network, should only be adopted if it provides a significant, quantifiable, and robust improvement in performance over the simpler alternative—an improvement that justifies the increased risk of overfitting and the loss of interpretability. This disciplined, stepwise approach is the most reliable way to arrive at a model that is not just accurate on paper, but also robust, trustworthy, and effective in a live operational setting. 2.5 Beyond the Model A successful machine learning implementation is built on more than just clever algorithms. While model selection is critical, it is only one component of a larger system. This section broadens the focus to the foundational, often non-technical, pillars that are essential for translating a promising model into a valuable and sustainable operational tool. These pillars — data quality, clear metrics, interpretability, and human collaboration—form the bedrock upon which successful data-driven process control is built. They also reveal that an ML project is not Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 17 merely a technical exercise, but a socio-technical endeavor that requires a holistic approach to succeed. 2.5.1 Pillar 1: Data is the Foundation The most fundamental principle of machine learning is that a model is only as good as the data from which it learns. The dataset must contain the patterns, relationships, and signals that the engineer wants the model to capture. If the necessary information is not present in the data, no amount of algorithmic sophistication can create it. This highlights that data collection is not a passive act of aggregation but may require active and deliberate experimental design. The biosolids optimization case study (Application 5) provides a powerful and instructive lesson on this topic from the entire project. Initial attempts to build a model to predict Total Solids (TS) from acoustic sensor data failed. The reason was not the algorithm, but the data itself. The digester feed process was so tightly and effectively controlled under normal operations that the historical data showed very little variability in TS concentrations. The model, when trained on this narrow range of data, simply learned to predict the average value and was incapable of forecasting deviations or extreme events. Success was only achieved after a dedicated experimental campaign was designed and executed in collaboration with plant operators. By intentionally and safely pushing the process to its operational boundaries, the team was able to generate the data variability necessary to train a robust and responsive model. This underscores a critical lesson: to build a model that can predict and manage process upsets, the training data must include examples of those upsets. 2.5.2 Pillar 2: Metrics To gauge the success of any engineering effort, it is vital to first define the finish line.
